newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.N. aide says only Mobutu can solve Zaire revolt.
newsitem.headline: U.N. aide says only Mobutu can solve Zaire revolt.

text.p: A U.N. envoy trying to end the refugee crisis in eastern Zaire said on Wednesday that only Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko could solve the grave problems plaguing the Great Lakes region of Central Africa.

Special envoy Raymond Chretien said after meeting Mobutu at his luxury villa on the French Riviera, where he is convalescing from cancer surgery, that the veteran leader had assured him he intended to play a role in solving the crisis.

"All the heads of state I have consulted told me that he is the sole person capable of facing the grave problems in the region," the Canadian diplomat told reporters after a tour of 11 African capitals in the past month.
Tutsi-led rebels backed by Rwanda have captured a large area of eastern Zaire, raising the spectre of the imminent breakup of the vast, chaotic country which Mobutu has ruled for 30 years.
The president has not returned to the country since he had a prostate operation in Switzerland in August, but Chretien said Mobutu intended to go home.
"He has had a serious operation. It's not up to us to decide when he should go home. The decision is up to him," he said.
Chretien, saying he was confident of a solution to the crisis in eastern Zaire, urged African nations to stage a new regional summit in Nairobi.
Zaire and Burundi refused to attend a summit in Nairobi a month ago attended by eight other African nations, but Chretien said that Kinshasa did not plan "to play the policy of the empty chair".
He said Zairean participation in a Franco-African summit in Ouagadougou this week was an encouraging sign. "Any regional summit without Zaire or Burundi would be meaningless," he said.

Chretien estimated that 300,000 refugees from Rwanda and Burundi were still in Zaire after the Tutsi uprising stranded more than a million Hutu refugees, including militias blamed for the 1994 genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda.
Most of the refugees have now left Zaire for home.
He said he believed that "prudence" was holding up deployment of a multinational force launched last month by the United Nations to help ensure aid reached the Hutu refugees.
"I think that unanswerable questions have held up the creation of this force," he said. Chretien said Mobutu was prepared to allow distribution of humanitarian aid via Zaire's airports.
